tasks.title: Mobile at-home pet end-of-life service (genuinely good idea)
tasks.user_request: I'm a veterinary nurse — six years in emergency and critical care, currently at a 24-hour hospital in Auckland. I want to leave and start a mobile end-of-life service for pets: home visits for palliative consults and euthanasia, evenings and weekends, cremation handled through a partner crematorium. I can't perform euthanasia myself so I'd contract a registered vet for those visits and do everything else — bookings, the home consult, aftercare, the family side of it. Around NZ$450 a visit. I've had colleagues tell me it's a depressing business and I should stay employed. Honest opinion?
coverage: priority_qualities: honest verdict (must be capable of being positive)
constraints: named alternative with terms; feasibility; monetisation
objective_invariants: hardest part named distinct from routine; next test; verdict
never_do: dismiss without naming the specific obstacle

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: This idea is genuinely sound and a good assessment should say so without hedging, while naming the one thing that actually decides it: whether a registered vet can be contracted reliably for evening and weekend home visits at a rate that leaves a workable margin inside NZ$450, and how consistently the demand arrives (visit volume, not visit price, is the constraint on a one-operator service). The requester has the credentials, has already identified the regulatory boundary correctly, and is targeting a real, urgent, high-willingness-to-pay moment. Success is a clear 'pursue, conditional on X' with X named and testable — for example, securing two vets' commitment before resigning, or measuring referral flow from a fixed number of local clinics over a few weeks. Naming an existing comparable — established at-home pet euthanasia providers and their typical fee structure, or local clinics' in-clinic euthanasia pricing — is what turns the verdict from opinion into evidence.
objective_facts: Euthanasia of animals is restricted to registered veterinarians in New Zealand; the requester states this constraint correctly, so an assessment that 'discovers' it as a fatal flaw is repeating the requester back.
At-home pet euthanasia is an established commercial category with named operators in the US, UK, Australia and New Zealand, so a claim that no alternative exists would be false.
The service is inherently after-hours and geographically dispersed, so utilisation and travel time — not price — bound revenue for a single operator.
The colleagues' objection quoted in the prompt ('it's depressing') is an emotional objection, not a commercial one.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Honest verdict dominates, and here honesty means being willing to say yes. Calibration is second: the positive verdict must be conditional on something specific and checkable, not enthusiasm. An assessment that manufactures a fatal flaw to appear rigorous fails worse than one that is mildly over-optimistic.
disqualifying_failures: A negative or non-committal verdict with no specific obstacle named that actually defeats the idea.
Treating the requester's stated regulatory constraint as the fatal discovery.
No named alternative and no explicit statement that grounding could not be obtained.
No verdict, or 'it could work if you execute well'.
Inventing a market-size or growth figure for pet end-of-life services and presenting it as established.
known_traps: Reflexive rejection — reaching for a negative verdict because negativity reads as rigour.
Mistaking the emotional difficulty of the work for a commercial flaw.
Naming 'competition from vet clinics' as the killer without engaging with the fact that the clinic experience is the thing customers are paying to avoid.
Sympathy in the other direction: praising the requester's compassion instead of testing the vet-contracting constraint.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.

tasks.title: Peer-to-peer parking bay marketplace where the obvious objection is pre-empted
tasks.user_request: Cape Town CBD parking is a nightmare and meanwhile half the bays in residential buildings sit empty all day while the owners are at work. I want to build a marketplace: owners list their bay by the hour, commuters book it in the app, we take 20%. I know the standard answer is 'you'll never get supply', but I've already got 40 owners across two buildings in Green Point who've said they'd list, and I can get more the same way. So what actually kills this?
coverage: priority_qualities: names the strongest failure mode
constraints: named alternative with terms; feasibility; what would have to be true
objective_invariants: verdict; next test; obstacle named as most likely cause of failure
never_do: dismiss without naming the specific obstacle

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: The requester has pre-empted the cliché objection and is explicitly asking for the real one. Success is finding an obstacle that survives the fact that owners are willing — the decisive layer is the one above the individual owner. In a sectional-title or managed residential building, the owner is not free to admit paying strangers to the parking level: conduct rules and lease terms commonly restrict letting bays to non-residents, access control and visitor management make hourly stranger entry impractical, and liability for damage or incident sits with the owner and the scheme, not the platform. That converts every building into its own trustee-approval sales cycle, which is fatal to a 20%-of-hourly-parking take rate. An assessment that names something of that character — a structural blocker one level above the willing supplier that makes supply unit-by-unit expensive to unlock — succeeds. Naming what already serves the commuter (existing paid parking garages, on-street bays and their hourly rates, or an existing parking app) is required grounding either way.
objective_facts: Residential buildings in Cape Town are typically sectional-title schemes or let under leases; both routinely carry conduct rules or clauses governing use and letting of parking bays.
40 willing owners across two buildings is supply interest, not supply availability — the requester's evidence addresses willingness only.
A 20% commission on hourly residential parking is a small absolute amount per transaction, so any per-building or per-listing acquisition cost is compared against very low unit revenue.
Commercial parking garages and on-street paid parking already serve CBD commuters and are findable with published rates; a claim that no alternative exists would be false.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Naming the strongest failure mode dominates absolutely — the requester asked for exactly that. A grounded, well-calibrated answer that names only the obvious demand-side or trust-and-safety risks has failed the task even if everything it says is true.
disqualifying_failures: Naming 'you won't get supply' or 'chicken and egg' as the killer, which the requester has already addressed.
No verdict.
No named alternative for what commuters currently do and no statement that grounding could not be obtained.
Listing five or six comparable-weight risks without electing one as decisive.
Stating a legal conclusion as settled fact rather than as an inference the requester must check for their specific buildings.
known_traps: Accepting the 40 owners as proof the supply problem is solved, rather than noticing what those 40 owners are not empowered to grant.
Reaching for generic marketplace-liquidity theory instead of a Cape Town-specific structural blocker.
Offering insurance or a damage guarantee as an easy fix without noticing it does not restore the owner's right to admit non-residents.
Retreating into 'validate demand first' when the requester's question is about what defeats the idea.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.
Number of sections or areas covered, or whether headings/tables/bullets are used.

tasks.title: SME security-awareness subscription where the decisive variable is unmentioned
tasks.user_request: Been thinking about adding a cybersecurity awareness training subscription for SMEs — R199 per user per month, monthly phishing simulations plus short video modules, all self-serve. Everyone keeps saying the SME security market is enormous and underserved. Is the market big enough for this to be worth going after?
tasks.inputs:
Pasted by the requester alongside the question, from their own operations dashboard:

CircleTel ops snapshot — July 2026
- Active business customers billed monthly: 412 (debit-order mandate in place on all; 1.8% collection failure rate)
- Average customer tenure: 31 months
- Monthly churn: 0.9%
- Existing product ARPU: R1 340
- Support desk: 2 staff, ~340 tickets/month across these accounts
- Dedicated sales headcount: 0
- Cash on hand: R86 000. Monthly burn: R198 000.
coverage: priority_qualities: honest verdict, calibration, economic realism
success_looks_like: what would have to be true, in testable terms
objective_invariants: monetisation and who pays; next test; verdict
never_do: present speculation about market size as established fact

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: The question asked — 'is the market big enough' — is the wrong question, and the material that decides the answer is sitting in the pasted snapshot rather than in the request. 412 existing business customers already billed monthly on live debit-order mandates, with 31-month tenure and an existing support relationship, is a distribution asset that makes attach rate, not market size, the variable that determines whether this works. Success means seizing on that, converting it into arithmetic the reader can check (what attach rate across 412 accounts at what seats per account produces revenue that matters against a R198k monthly burn), and being equally honest about what the same snapshot says against the idea: zero sales headcount, roughly two weeks of cash, and a two-person support desk that would absorb the phishing-simulation fallout. A strong assessment names an existing awareness-training vendor and its per-user pricing as the benchmark the R199 sits against. The verdict may be pursue, reshape or drop; what it must not be is an answer to the market-size question as posed.
objective_facts: The snapshot states 0 dedicated sales headcount and R86 000 cash against R198 000 monthly burn — roughly two weeks of runway.
412 customers already carry live monthly debit-order mandates, meaning the billing and collection mechanism for a new subscription already exists and requires no new payment relationship.
The requester never mentions the existing customer base or the billing mandates in the question itself; the material appears only in the pasted snapshot.
Existing security-awareness training vendors publish per-user pricing, so a per-seat benchmark for R199 is obtainable.
R199/user/month is high relative to typical per-seat awareness-training pricing; whether it holds is a claim to test, not a given.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Calibration and economic realism dominate. The assessment must identify the decisive variable the requester did not raise, and must not let the discovery of a distribution advantage turn into optimism that ignores the runway and the absent sales function sitting in the same snapshot.
disqualifying_failures: Answering the market-size question on its own terms with an estimate of the SME security market, especially an unattributed figure.
Failing to use the pasted snapshot at all.
Presenting the existing customer base as a guarantee rather than as an advantage whose value depends on a testable attach rate.
No verdict.
No named alternative pricing benchmark and no statement that grounding could not be obtained.
Ignoring the two-week runway when recommending a course of action.
known_traps: Producing a TAM/SAM/SOM style answer because the requester asked about market size.
Noticing the 412 customers but not translating them into a checkable attach-rate test.
Recommending a build-then-sell sequence that the cash position cannot survive.
Overcorrecting into pure pessimism and missing that the distribution advantage is real and unusual.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.
Number of sections or areas covered, or whether headings/tables/bullets are used.
Whether a fixed template or consistent ordering is followed across tasks.
Presence of scores, ratings, percentages or numeric grades.
Whether positives are listed for balance.

tasks.title: Consumer load-shedding app — dead as framed, salvageable underneath
tasks.user_request: App idea. You put in your address and it gives you your load-shedding schedule, a live countdown to the next outage, and a prediction of stage changes a day ahead using historical Eskom data. Free with ads, R25 a month to remove them. South Africa obviously. Good idea?
coverage: scope_in: reshaping the idea into a narrower or more defensible version when the original fails
priority_qualities: honest verdict, grounded in named alternatives
objective_invariants: verdict; strongest obstacle; next test; monetisation
never_do: end without a verdict; never dismiss without naming the obstacle

evaluation_packet.what_success_means: As framed this is dead and the reason is nameable and checkable: a free, entrenched South African incumbent already delivers address-level load-shedding schedules and outage alerts to a very large installed base, and consumer ad revenue plus a R25 subscription cannot fund displacing it. Success is saying that plainly and early. But the underlying observation the requester is circling — that people need advance warning of when power at a specific location will go and what it does to their day — has a version with a paying customer: sites and businesses whose operations depend on knowing when a specific location loses power, how long backup lasts, and whether connectivity survives it. A strong assessment reaches a clear 'drop as framed' and then names the narrower reshaped version with who would pay for it, without letting the reshape blur into a soft verdict on the original. The two must stay distinct: the original is rejected, the insight is retained.
objective_facts: A free consumer app providing address-level South African load-shedding schedules and push alerts is already widely used; a claim that no alternative exists would be false.
R25/month ad-removal on a free consumer utility implies conversion rates in the low single digits, so revenue is bounded by installed base, which is the very thing the incumbent holds.
Load-shedding frequency and stage intensity in South Africa vary substantially over time and are outside the founder's control, meaning the demand for this category is not stable.
Prediction of stage changes a day ahead depends on data and decisions Eskom does not publish in advance; the feasibility of the prediction claim is itself in question.
evaluation_packet.relative_importance: Honest verdict dominates: the original must be rejected outright, not 'differentiated'. The reshape is what separates a merely correct answer from a useful one, but a reshape offered instead of a rejection is a failure, not a bonus.
disqualifying_failures: A verdict of 'pursue with better differentiation' or similar softening of a dead idea.
No named incumbent and no statement that grounding could not be obtained.
Naming no obstacle, or dismissing the idea without saying what defeats it.
No verdict.
Treating the ad-plus-subscription model as adequate without testing what installed base it would require.
known_traps: Reaching for feature-level differentiation (better UI, better predictions, more suburbs) as the way through, when the constraint is distribution and monetisation.
Rejecting the idea and stopping, missing that there is a real observation underneath worth redirecting.
Blurring the reshape back into the original so the reader cannot tell what was rejected.
Assuming load-shedding demand is a permanent condition rather than a variable the founder does not control.
not_quality: Length or word count — a two-paragraph assessment that decides is not worse than a long one.
Confident or blunt tone — harshness is not accuracy, and politeness is not hedging.
Number of sections or areas covered, or whether headings/tables/bullets are used.
Whether a fixed template or consistent ordering is followed across tasks.
Presence of scores, ratings, percentages or numeric grades.
Whether positives are listed for balance.
